_comment: Deterministic fixtures for the Weakness Radar topic-health algorithm (TASK-2201).
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. The scoring rules are implemented twice on purpose: in Java
(backend/.../service/TopicHealthService.java) for signed-in students, and in TypeScript
(mobile/src/intelligence/topicHealth.ts) for signed-out students whose attempts never
reach a server. That duplication follows the precedent this codebase already set for the
mastery ladder, but it can drift. This file is the one agreed statement of what the
algorithm should produce, so both copies can be checked against the same cases rather
The Java side asserts against it in TopicHealthScoringTest. The mobile side has no test
runner in this project (no jest/vitest is configured), so its copy is verified by reading
and on the emulator - stated plainly rather than implied.
Every case maps to a numbered requirement in the supplied spec's section 23. Expectations
are deliberately partial: a case asserts the thing it is about (a state, a trend, a bound,
a relation to another case) and not every number, so tuning an unrelated weight does not
produce a wall of false failures.
Event fields: eventId groups answers from one sitting (consistency is measured across
sittings, so this matters); daysAgo is relative to the injected 'now'; difficulty is a
difficulty_levels code, or null for 'no metadata'; pyq marks previous-year questions.

cases.name: one-wrong-answer-is-not-a-weakness
cases.why: A single mistake must never produce a weakness. This is the failure mode the whole evidence-level idea exists to prevent.

cases.name: few-attempts-stay-insufficient
cases.why: Four answered questions is under the evidence floor, however badly they went.

cases.name: sustained-poor-performance-needs-attention
cases.why: Repeated weak sessions on reliable evidence is the one case that should assert a problem.

cases.name: sustained-good-performance-is-strong
cases.why: The mirror of the case above: the same volume answered well must come out strong.

cases.name: recent-improvement-changes-the-trend
cases.why: 50% historically, 87% recently. The trend must read IMPROVING even though the state may well be STRONG by then - trend and state are separate dimensions (spec 12).

cases.name: improving-from-weak-is-not-labelled-weak
cases.why: Spec 6 and 12's own example: 30% historically, 60% recently, health around the low 60s. Must be IMPROVING, never NEEDS_ATTENTION - this is the case where a naive accuracy threshold gets it wrong.

cases.name: historical-strength-then-decline-needs-revision
cases.why: 90% historically, 50% recently. This must be its own finding, not flattened into NEEDS_ATTENTION - the student once knew this, which changes what they should do about it.

cases.name: variance-steady-baseline
cases.why: 76 correct out of 100, spread evenly. Paired with the case below, which has the SAME total accuracy but swings wildly - the two must not read as the same preparation state.

cases.name: variance-erratic-same-average
cases.why: Also 76 of 100, but 100/40/100/40/100. Consistency must collapse and confidence must end up strictly below the steady case - spec 10 and 11.

cases.name: difficulty-easy-questions-at-60-percent
cases.why: 60% on easy questions. Paired with the hard-question case below: identical accuracy, and the hard one must score higher - but by a bounded amount (spec 7 forbids hard questions swinging the score).

cases.name: difficulty-hard-questions-at-60-percent
cases.why: Same 60%, on hard questions. Should read better than the easy case, and the whole difference must stay inside the difficulty term's bounded contribution.

cases.name: missing-difficulty-metadata-falls-back-safely
cases.why: Spec 21: no difficulty metadata must drop the signal, not be bucketed as medium. The topic still gets a health score from the signals that do exist.

cases.name: pyq-weakness-lowers-health
cases.why: 80% on ordinary questions, 20% on real previous-year ones. Paired with the identical-answers-untagged case below: the ONLY difference is the PYQ tag, so the gap isolates the PYQ signal exactly.

cases.name: pyq-control-same-answers-untagged
cases.why: Identical answers with the PYQ tag removed. Health must come out HIGHER than the tagged case (the PYQ signal is real) but not wildly so (spec 8: PYQ must not override everything else).

cases.name: too-few-pyqs-drops-the-pyq-signal
cases.why: Spec 21: missing PYQ evidence excludes the signal rather than assuming anything. Four PYQ answers is under the floor.

cases.name: no-timing-data-produces-no-speed-signal
cases.why: Spec 9: a missing signal must not become fake data. No fixture carries timing, so speed must be absent - not 1.0x, not a neutral 50 folded into health.

cases.name: strong-topic-survives-one-mistake
cases.why: Fifty answers at 100%, then one wrong. Must stay STRONG. If a single error can move a well-established topic out of STRONG, the recency weighting is too aggressive.

cases.name: one-bad-session-does-not-destroy-health
cases.why: Sixty answers at 83%, then one six-question session at 17%. Health should fall - that is real evidence - but nowhere near NEEDS_ATTENTION.

cases.name: recent-evidence-baseline
cases.why: Thirty answers at 30%, all inside the recent window. Paired with the eight-month-old case below, which has IDENTICAL answers - so the confidence gap between them is purely the effect of age.

cases.name: very-old-evidence-lowers-confidence
why: The same thirty answers, eight months old. Spec 21 asks for old data to be de-emphasised rather than treated as current, so the requirement is stated as a RELATION to the fresh twin above, not as an absolute bound - an absolute number here would just be asserting the current weights back at themselves.

Worth knowing what it actually produces: confidence lands around 71, down from around 89 fresh. That is deliberately still above the floor at which a verdict is asserted, so the topic does read as NEEDS_ATTENTION. That is the right answer rather than a gap: if the student had practised this since, there would be newer evidence, so 'you were weak here and have not been back' is both well-evidenced and actionable. What makes it honest is the staleRecentWindow flag, which raises a STALE_PRACTICE reason code so the UI says the diagnosis rests on older practice instead of implying it is current.
